Lead story

Ray: Okay, so the problem. Melt-pool monitoring is central to qualifying metal additive manufacturing, and the authors say there's no public event-camera benchmark for it. Until now.

Ada: Quick reminder for everyone. What's an event camera?

Ray: Instead of reading out full frames, each pixel reports only when its brightness changes, with microsecond timing. So you get the fast timing that printing transients demand, at a fraction of the data rate.

Ada: Got it. So what did they actually build?

Ray: A release called SynAM-E, short for Synthetic AM Events. It has eighty-five event shards, which are chunks of data, from fifteen sources across eight institutions. They describe it as physics calibrated, with public baselines and fixed evaluation splits across machines.

Ada: And the headline result?

Ray: On a single-machine case study, event-based spatial monitoring scored zero point eight seven four macro F one, versus zero point eight six three for dense frames. Macro F one is a score that averages performance across classes equally. The absolute intensity that events throw away added only zero point zero zero six when fused back in.

Ray: Then on the NIST Additive Manufacturing Metrology Testbed build, a near-sensor event-rate counter recovered a five hundred twenty-eight point seven hertz intensity oscillation, confirmed against raw frames, with about three hundred eighty times less sensor readout. And a compact spiking model with ninety-three thousand parameters ran at fifteen times lower modeled inference energy, for a cost of zero point zero seven three macro F one.

Ada: Okay, here's my big one. It's simulated. How close are simulated events to what a real sensor does?

Ray: The story lists that as an open question. The abstract says physics calibrated, but it doesn't put a number on the match.

Ada: And that fifteen times energy figure is modeled, not measured on hardware.

Ray: Right, the abstract says modeled. Nothing more than that.

Ada: One more. A classifier can cheat by just learning which camera took the picture.

Ray: They anticipated that. Every cross-source task has a built-in trust test against camera identity shortcuts. Process-type classification passes. Material classification stays confounded by camera band, and the authors document that openly.

Ada: I respect a benchmark that admits where it fails.

Ray: Same. Why it matters: shared splits across machines mean different groups can finally compare methods on equal footing.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to materials. First, GMMag, a workflow that generates crystal structures together with the magnetic moment on each atomic site. It's a conditional variational autoencoder, with a graph neural network encoder and a transformer decoder.

Ada: What's the trick?

Ray: Gaussian-mixture sampling steers generation toward chosen chemical and magnetic targets without retraining. In two separate ten-million-draw runs, it found neodymium-containing candidates with new formulas, negative formation energies, and high estimated saturation magnetization.

Ada: Estimated, from a surrogate. And stable plus magnetized isn't the same as a good permanent magnet. Nothing here shows anisotropy.

Ray: Fair. The abstract doesn't claim it.

Ray: Next, a caution for anyone using machine learning to find phase transitions. Learning by confusion looks for a peak in an accuracy curve and calls it the transition. The authors show that peak closely follows the maximum of the Fisher information, a statistical measure of how sharply the data distinguish nearby temperatures.

Ada: So what's the catch?

Ray: The same configurations on temperature grids uniform in T, in log T, or in one over T can give different finite-size trajectories. They tested Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts, and Baxter-Wu models.

Ada: So how you space your samples can shift your answer. Noted.

Ray: Last, crystALL, which builds candidate sets of metastable structures from about five million relaxed structures, rather than chasing stability alone. The abstract is cut off, so validation details are unconfirmed.

Metal printing

Ray: Staying with event cameras, there's a careful characterization of an IMX636 sensor under sinusoidal and pulsed light. First-event latency is below five microseconds.

Ray: But the full response lasts much longer, because of photoreceptor dynamics, refractory behavior, and readout serialization. So microsecond timestamps don't guarantee faithful waveform reconstruction at high frequencies, or in dense bright scenes like melt pools.

First public event-camera melt-pool benchmark includes cross-machine splits and NIST AMMT

Mohamad Yazan Sadoun · arXiv (Cornell University) · 9/10

The SynAM-E release provides 85 simulated event-camera data shards from 15 sources, with fixed splits across machines. The abstract reports that event-based monitoring matches dense frames (0.874 vs 0.863 macro-F1), and that an event-rate counter recovered a 528.7 Hz oscillation on AMMT with about 380 times less readout. Open questions include how closely simulated events match real sensor behavior, and the authors note that material classification is confounded by camera band.

Learning-by-confusion peak tracks Fisher information and shifts with how data are sampled

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 9/10

The abstract reports that the learning-by-confusion peak follows the Fisher information maximum. It also reports that temperature grids spaced uniformly in T, ln T, or 1/T produce different finite-size pseudocritical trajectories, tested on Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts and Baxter-Wu models. The result suggests that how temperature points are spaced can matter for machine-learning phase mapping.

GMMag generates crystals with site-resolved moments, steerable toward chemical and magnetic targets

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 8/10

A conditional VAE with a graph encoder and transformer decoder generates structures with per-site magnetic moments. Gaussian-mixture sampling steers it toward chosen targets without retraining. The abstract reports Nd-containing candidates with negative formation energy and high estimated saturation magnetization, but stability plus a surrogate magnetization is not evidence of magnetic anisotropy.

IMX636 event sensor: first-event latency under 5 µs, but full response is much slower

arXiv · event-based vision · 7/10

This is a quantitative characterization of an IMX636 event camera under sinusoidal and pulsed light. The abstract reports first-event latencies below 5 µs, but the full response lasts much longer because of photoreceptor dynamics, refractory behavior and readout serialization. That suggests microsecond timestamps don't guarantee faithful waveform reconstruction at high frequencies or in dense, bright scenes such as melt pools.

Spatiotemporal CNN–state-space model predicts weld penetration from weld-pool images

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 8/10

The model takes top weld-pool images plus welding parameters to predict penetration state, depth and cross-section morphology. The abstract reports 99.35% state accuracy and 1.79 mm depth error. It is about laser welding rather than LPBF, and it does not say how the test set was split, which matters because random splits can inflate accuracy numbers.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Neutron-diffraction magnetic structure of a Prussian blue analogue, with a Monte Carlo vacancy model

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports the magnetic structure of Co[Cr(CN)6]2/3·zH2O from neutron powder diffraction, with no sign of magnetostriction at ordering. A simple Monte Carlo model suggests the ordering is robust to vacancy correlations, with only minor effects in the critical region. It is not a cerium paper, but it is a small example of simulation tied to measured magnetic order.

crystALL builds metastable candidate ensembles beyond the convex hull

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The method uses about 5 million relaxed structures from OPTIMADE and MPDD, applying species substitution, pySIPFENN feature-space analysis and clustering to produce candidate sets for validation. It is not magnetism-aware, but its idea of keeping metastable diversity rather than stability alone is notable. The abstract is cut off, so its validation details are unconfirmed.

Determinant QMC shows gauge-mediated Kondo breakdown in a U(1) heavy-fermion model

Physical Review Letters · 5/10

Sign-problem-free determinant quantum Monte Carlo finds a heavy-fermion metal and a Kondo-breakdown metal with different Luttinger volumes. This is background theory on f-electron systems rather than a direct tool for materials screening. The model is minimal, a spin chain coupled to Dirac electrons, so how far it maps onto real cerium compounds is an open question.

Valence transition and phase coexistence in substituted EuPd2Si2

Physical Review Materials · 5/10

This Phys. Rev. Materials paper studies the valence transition in EuPd2Si2, which responds to temperature, pressure and magnetic field. It is relevant to rare-earth valence physics, which also matters for cerium. Only a truncated abstract is available, so the main findings are unconfirmed.

Additive Manufacturing

Euler pitches in-situ monitoring with a sensor LPBF users already own

3D Printing Industry · 5/10

The article opens with a familiar problem: CT results often arrive weeks after a build, showing defects that began around layer 400. It is a vendor piece promoting an in-situ monitoring approach, so its claims deserve skepticism. The summary doesn't say whether any ground-truth validation or per-build testing is described.

Tracking individual defects in SLM IN718 through XCT to follow damage evolution

J. Manufacturing Processes · 4/10

No abstract is available, so the details are unconfirmed. From the title, the work follows individual defects in SLM IN718 with X-ray computed tomography (XCT) to track how damage evolves. That makes it a possible reference point for CT-based ground truth in monitoring studies.

Physics-guided FEM plus GPR predicts DED melt-pool geometry and grain transition

J. Manufacturing Processes · 5/10

The abstract reports a finite-element model calibrated on single-track melt-pool measurements, with errors under 6%, which then generated data for a Gaussian-process regression surrogate with R² values of 0.992 and 0.996. The study covers single tracks of an in-situ alloyed high-entropy alloy in DED, so it has no monitoring component. The useful idea is simulation as a physics prior, though performance outside the calibrated conditions remains an open question.

On-chip DVS optical-flow sensor claims 303× lower power than FPGA-accelerated DVS

arXiv · event-based vision · 5/10

The pixel-level circuit compares ON and OFF events over time differences and outputs flow vectors directly, at microsecond-level latency. It is hardware context for event sensing and has no melt-pool test. Whether the 303× power figure comes from measured silicon or a projection is unclear, since the abstract also mentions a memristor variant.

Theoretical Physics

Massive phase of 2D Heisenberg model survives small anisotropy

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 7/10

The paper proves that, at any temperature, spin correlations still decay exponentially under small anisotropy, including easy-plane and single-ion terms. In plain terms, a slight departure from perfect symmetry does not immediately produce long-range order or a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless (BKT) phase at finite temperature. The authors say their bound is weaker than the physically predicted behavior.

Bootstrap proof of Néel order in the 2D S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 8/10

Long-range order in this model had never been rigorously proven, despite strong numerical evidence. The authors prove it for a discrete set of anisotropy values, including the isotropic point, using Kennedy–Lieb–Shastry-type bounds and certified variational energy bounds from matrix product states. It is rigorous mathematics about the kind of spin model that Monte Carlo studies usually simulate.

Detection times can't be localized observables in quantum field theory

arXiv · high-energy theory · 6/10

The moment a detector clicks is usually treated as a local event, but the authors argue that under natural requirements, the observable describing that time cannot be confined to any bounded region of spacetime, even if the record itself is local. That challenges the assumption that microcausality alone guarantees measurements cannot send signals. Only the abstract is available, so how general the 'natural requirements' are remains to be checked.

Bell violations may show that history is relevant, not that locality fails

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

The paper argues that relativity should limit how an event's probability depends on probabilities of events in its causal past, a condition that differs from Bell's local-causality criterion. The author contends the two coincide only if history is irrelevant, so Bell violations need not conflict with relativity. It is a philosophical argument rather than a new experiment, and one position in a long-running debate.

Policy & Funding

GM–eVAC split highlights demand-side risk in US magnet buildout

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 6/10

Benchmark Mineral Intelligence points to demand risk, not only supply risk, in building US magnet capacity. Only the headline is available, so the specifics are unconfirmed. The point matters for rare-earth magnets generally, since new capacity depends on offtake as well as mining.

Rare Earth Exchanges explains China's defense supply-chain vulnerability for rare earths

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 8/10

This is a headline-only item, so its content is unconfirmed. It addresses rare-earth security, focusing on China's defense supply-chain vulnerability. The summary does not say which elements or magnet grades are covered.

South Korea's LS Cable to invest $262M in rare earth magnets

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 6/10

UPI reports a $262M investment in rare-earth magnets by South Korea's LS Cable, which adds to non-Chinese magnet capacity. Only the headline is available, so the product type and timeline are unconfirmed. It is not yet clear whether the investment covers magnet manufacturing or upstream materials.

GKN Aerospace gets first Nadcap accreditation for laser wire DED

3D Printing Industry · 5/10

3D Printing Industry reports that GKN is the first company to earn Nadcap accreditation for laser wire directed energy deposition. It is a qualification milestone in DED rather than LPBF. The summary doesn't say which monitoring or inspection requirements the accreditation involves.

Fun fact

Scientists report a possible loophole in the laws that normally keep black holes from splitting, suggesting extremely fast-spinning ones might divide in two. If real, it would be a new black-hole phenomenon that future telescopes could in principle detect. The claim comes from a press summary, so the details are unconfirmed. source
